Torsemide exerts its potent natriuretic and diuretic efficacy by selectively binding to and inhibiting which of the following apical membrane cotransporters located in the medullary and cortical thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

options.A: Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2)
options.B: Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC)
options.C: Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC)
options.D: Na+/H+ antiporter isoform 3 (NHE3)
options.E: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Torsemide (along with furosemide and bumetanide) is a loop diuretic that reversibly and competitively binds to the chloride-binding site of the apical Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of Henle's loop. Compared to furosemide, torsemide has superior, more predictable oral bioavailability (~80-100% vs. 10-90% for furosemide) and a longer duration of action, making it highly effective in advanced heart failure patients who develop intestinal mucosal edema and variable absorption on oral furosemide.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Renal System: Pharmacology of Diuretics and Vasopressin Regulators
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 58-year-old female with long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease presents for medication optimization. Her current medications include metformin and lisinopril. Despite maximally tolerated lisinopril, her blood pressure is 144/88 mm Hg and her urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) is 420 mg/g. Her nephrologist initiates empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor. SGLT2 inhibitors act primarily in the early proximal convoluted tubule to induce mild natriuresis, osmotic glycosuria, and reduce intraglomerular hypertension. Which of the following transport and hemodynamic alterations directly accounts for the sustained reduction in intraglomerular pressure and long-term renal protection provided by SGLT2 inhibitors?

options.A: Inhibition of proximal SGLT2 increases delivery of NaCl to the macula densa, restoring tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) to trigger afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and lower glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.B: Selective blockade of distal ENaC channels stimulates systemic prostaglandin synthesis, inducing profound efferent arteriolar vasodilation
options.C: Competitive antagonism of basolateral V2 receptors in collecting ducts drops medullary interstitial pressure
options.D: Direct inhibition of thick ascending limb NKCC2 cotransporters prevents macula densa depolarization and suppresses renin
options.E: Downregulation of proximal NHE3 antiporters directly stimulates renal sympathetic nerves to constrict the renal vein

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: In diabetic nephropathy, chronic proximal tubular hyper-reabsorption of glucose and sodium via upregulated SGLT2 cotransporters reduces downstream NaCl delivery to the macula densa. The macula densa senses this falsely as low perfusion, blunting tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) and inducing inappropriate afferent arteriolar vasodilation, which drives intraglomerular hypertension and progressive nephron loss. SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) inhibit SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule, increasing NaCl and fluid delivery to the macula densa. Macula densa cells take up NaCl via NKCC2, release adenosine, and activate adenosine A1 receptors on adjacent vascular smooth muscle, restoring normal TGF. This triggers afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, immediately reducing glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC) and albuminuria, thereby conferring profound, long-term renal and cardiovascular protection.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Renal System: Pharmacology of Diuretics and Vasopressin Regulators
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 49-year-old male with chronic hepatitis C cirrhosis and moderate ascites is started on spironolactone monotherapy (100 mg daily). Two weeks later, he presents with mild lethargy and muscle weakness. Serum chemistry reveals: sodium = 136 mEq/L, potassium = 5.8 mEq/L (hyperkalemia), chloride = 106 mEq/L, bicarbonate = 18 mEq/L, and arterial pH = 7.31 (hyperchloremic normal-anion gap metabolic acidosis). Serum creatinine is stable at 1.0 mg/dL. By competitively inhibiting cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptors in late distal tubule and collecting duct principal cells and alpha-intercalated cells, what specific physiological transport alterations explain this drug-induced Type 4 renal tubular acidosis (RTA)?

options.A: Downregulation of apical ENaC channels collapses the lumen-negative transepithelial voltage, extinguishing passive ROMK/BK potassium excretion and alpha-intercalated cell H+-ATPase proton pumping
options.B: Direct activation of proximal carbonic anhydrase causes massive proximal tubular bicarbonate wasting
options.C: Selective inhibition of the apical Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCC) in the DCT promotes active bicarbonate secretion
options.D: Inhibition of basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase in the thick ascending limb reverses the corticomedullary osmotic gradient
options.E: Blockade of aquaporin-2 water channels triggers rapid back-diffusion of unbuffered carbonic acid into cortical capillaries

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Aldosterone normally stimulates the synthesis and apical membrane insertion of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in principal cells, as well as stimulating apical H+-ATPase pumps in alpha-intercalated cells. Electrogenic sodium reabsorption through ENaC generates a negative luminal potential (-30 to -50 mV) that provides the primary electrical driving force pulling K+ through ROMK/BK channels into the lumen and facilitating H+ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells. Spironolactone competitively antagonizes the mineralocorticoid receptor, downregulating ENaC. Loss of electrogenic sodium entry collapses the lumen-negative transepithelial potential to near 0 mV. Without this negative driving force, potassium exit and proton extrusion are impaired, resulting in hyperkalemia and decreased net acid excretion, manifesting as drug-induced Type 4 (hyperkalemic) renal tubular acidosis.

usmle_practice_problems.lecture_title: Renal System: Pharmacology of Diuretics and Vasopressin Regulators
usmle_practice_problems.vignette: A 72-year-old male with severe peripheral vascular disease and recurrent calcium-containing radiopaque kidney stones is treated with indapamide (2.5 mg daily) for hypertension. Indapamide is an indoline-derived thiazide-like diuretic. While indapamide effectively lowers blood pressure and reduces urinary calcium excretion by inhibiting apical NCC in the distal convoluted tubule, which of the following metabolic disturbances is a well-established, frequent adverse effect of thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics that requires routine biochemical monitoring?

options.A: Impaired glucose tolerance (hyperglycemia) due to inhibition of pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion and peripheral insulin resistance
options.B: Severe hypercalcemic crisis resulting from direct stimulation of parathyroid adenomas
options.C: Profound hyperkalemia resulting from proximal tubular organic anion retention
options.D: Severe hypermagnesemia due to upregulation of TRPM6 channels in the descending loop of Henle
options.E: Acute non-anion gap metabolic acidosis secondary to basolateral chloride-bicarbonate exchange failure

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (such as indapamide, chlorthalidone, and hydrochlorothiazide) are well known to induce hyperglycemia and worsen glycemic control in patients with diabetes mellitus or metabolic syndrome. The primary mechanism is mediated by thiazide-induced hypokalemia: low extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential of pancreatic beta-islet cells, which blunts ATP-sensitive potassium channel (K_ATP) closure and voltage-gated calcium entry, impairing glucose-stimulated insulin exocytosis. Additionally, thiazides can decrease peripheral tissue sensitivity to insulin. Routine monitoring of fasting plasma glucose and serum electrolytes is standard clinical practice.

options.A: 1) Furosemide selectively inhibits apical NKCC2 cotransporters in the thick ascending limb, delivering a massive load of fluid and NaCl to the distal nephron; in cirrhosis, baseline effective arterial underfilling drives maximal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis activation, which upregulates principal cell ENaC channels to reabsorb Na+ electrogenically, generating an intense lumen-negative transepithelial voltage that drives massive ROMK/BK potassium excretion and alpha-intercalated cell H+-ATPase proton pumping, establishing severe hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; 2) In response to profound extracellular hypokalemia (2.3 mEq/L), cells throughout the body—most critically proximal convoluted tubule epithelial cells—extrude intracellular K+ down its chemical gradient into the blood in exchange for extracellular H+ and Na+ entering the cell; 3) This transcellular cation shift induces paradoxical intracellular acidosis within proximal tubular cells despite severe systemic extracellular alkalemia (pH 7.58); intracellular acidosis directly stimulates mitochondrial phosphate-dependent glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase, accelerating the deamination of glutamine into alpha-ketoglutarate and generating massive quantities of ammonia (NH3/NH4+) that enter the renal venous blood; 4) Under systemic alkalemic conditions (pH 7.58), the Henderson-Hasselbalch equilibrium (pKa of NH4+/NH3 ~9.2) shifts rightward, markedly increasing the fraction of uncharged, highly lipid-soluble non-ionized ammonia (NH3); non-ionized NH3 freely diffuses across the lipophilic blood-brain barrier into cerebral astrocytes, where it is converted by glutamine synthetase into osmotically active glutamine, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, neurotransmission failure, asterixis, and coma; 5) Emergency management mandates immediate cessation of furosemide, aggressive intravenous repletion with potassium chloride (which replenishes intracellular K+, terminates the transcellular H+ influx, corrects proximal tubular intracellular acidosis, and shuts down renal ammoniagenesis), cautious isotonic volume restoration, and oral/rectal lactulose to acidify the colon and trap unabsorbable NH4+ in the stool
options.B: 1) Furosemide destroys medullary vasa recta capillaries, causing retrograde reflux of bile into renal lymphatics; 2) Hypokalemia causes ischemic necrosis of pancreatic islet alpha cells, terminating all glucagon secretion; 3) Proximal tubule cells reabsorb urea and convert it directly into gaseous nitric oxide; 4) Nitric oxide gas dissolves in cerebral spinal fluid to produce cavernous sinus thrombosis; 5) Management requires emergent surgical creation of a portocaval shunt followed by high-dose intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusions
options.C: 1) Furosemide binds basolateral V1a receptors in coronary vessels to induce acute cardiac shock; 2) Hypokalemia causes sudden rupture of skeletal muscle actin fibers, releasing pure myoglobin into the blood; 3) Proximal tubule cells convert filtered myoglobin into insoluble uric acid stones; 4) Uric acid crosses into cerebral ventricles and activates microglial NLRP3 inflammasomes; 5) Management consists of initiating daily pegloticase infusions and urgent peritoneal dialysis against a high-potassium bath
options.D: 1) High-dose loop diuresis stimulates macula densa cells to secrete massive amounts of somatostatin; 2) Somatostatin binds adrenal cortical cells, causing total suppression of cortisol; 3) Adrenal crisis causes proximal tubule cells to secrete bicarbonate into peritubular capillaries; 4) Extracellular alkalemia causes rapid precipitation of ammonia into radiolucent kidney stones; 5) Emergency management requires immediate intravenous acetazolamide boluses combined with high-dose spironolactone
options.E: 1) Furosemide competitively inhibits basolateral OAT1 transporters, trapping organic anions in systemic veins; 2) Trapped anions bind to cardiac troponin, causing acute left ventricular dilatation; 3) Renal tubules switch to paracellular ammonium reabsorption down a hydrostatic gradient; 4) Ionized NH4+ crosses the blood-brain barrier through aquaporin-4 water channels; 5) Management consists of performing emergent bilateral nephrectomy within 2 hours of presentation

usmle_practice_problems.rationale: This 5th-order problem integrates loop diuretic transport pharmacology, distal nephron electrogenic physiology, systemic acid-base buffering, renal tubular ammoniagenesis, neurovascular permeability biophysics, and emergency neurohepatology: (1) Diuretic-induced hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis: Furosemide blocks the apical Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb, flooding the distal tubule and collecting duct with fluid and NaCl. In cirrhotic patients with splanchnic arterial vasodilation and reduced effective circulating arterial volume, baseline secondary hyperaldosteronism is maximal. Excessive distal delivery stimulates rapid electrogenic sodium reabsorption via apical ENaC channels in principal cells. The resulting lumen-negative transepithelial voltage drives excessive potassium secretion via ROMK and BK channels (kaliuresis) and stimulates active proton secretion by alpha-intercalated cell apical H+-ATPase, generating severe hypokalemia (2.3 mEq/L) and metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.58, bicarbonate 42 mEq/L); (2) Transcellular ion exchange: To maintain extracellular potassium concentration, cells throughout the body—especially proximal convoluted tubule epithelial cells—extrude intracellular K+ down a steep concentration gradient in exchange for extracellular H+ and Na+ entering the cell; (3) Paradoxical intracellular acidosis & renal ammoniagenesis: This transcellular shift induces paradoxical intracellular acidosis within proximal tubular cells despite severe extracellular systemic alkalemia. Intracellular acidosis is the primary stimulus that allosterically and transcriptionally activates mitochondrial phosphate-dependent glutaminase (PDG) and glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) in the proximal tubule. These enzymes rapidly deaminate glutamine into alpha-ketoglutarate, producing two ammonium ions (NH4+) and two bicarbonate ions per glutamine. Because of this activation, renal ammoniagenesis surges dramatically, and large amounts of synthesized ammonia enter the renal veins and systemic circulation; (4) Diffusion across blood-brain barrier in alkalemia: In the blood, ammonia exists in equilibrium between charged ammonium (NH4+) and uncharged non-ionized ammonia (NH3) with a pKa of ~9.2. Charged NH4+ cannot cross the intact blood-brain barrier, whereas lipid-soluble NH3 freely diffuses across biological membranes. Under severe systemic alkalemia (pH 7.58), the Henderson-Hasselbalch equilibrium shifts rightward, significantly increasing the relative concentration of non-ionized NH3. This allows rapid diffusion of NH3 across the blood-brain barrier into brain tissue. Inside cerebral astrocytes, ammonia is metabolized by glutamine synthetase into glutamine; accumulating glutamine acts as an intracellular osmolyte, drawing water into astrocytes and inducing cerebral edema, astrocyte dysfunction, asterixis, and hepatic coma; (5) Evidence-based emergency resuscitation: Management mandates: (a) immediate cessation of loop diuretics to halt ongoing renal K+ and H+ wasting; (b) aggressive parenteral repletion of potassium chloride (KCl), which replenishes intracellular K+ pools, resolves proximal tubular intracellular acidosis, and shuts down renal ammoniagenesis; (c) cautious volume restoration with isotonic fluids to reverse prerenal azotemia; and (d) administration of lactulose, which is metabolized by colonic bacteria into organic acids (lactic and acetic acid), lowering colonic pH to protonate absorbable NH3 into unabsorbable NH4+ ('ammonia trapping') to be excreted in stool.
